description: An independent engineering crew focused on fault-tolerant systems, edge infrastructure, and data-driven solutions for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Driven by practical engineering principles, we transform raw space telemetry and open scientific datasets into resilient, high-performance tools built to operate under strict real-world constraints.
summary:
We developed ORION-MED (HEV-1), an offline-first medical monitoring and decision-support prototype for astronauts on long-duration lunar and Mars-transit missions. Built with Python (FastAPI, SQLite) and React (TypeScript), it unifies physiological vitals, cabin atmosphere sensors (ECLSS), a 10-second Psychomotor Vigilance Test (PVT), and cached NASA DONKI space weather context into one onboard interface.

To support non-physician crews, the software pairs a clickable Digital Human Twin with deterministic threshold rules, Master Caution and Master Warning alerts, spoken and tonal cues, step-by-step countermeasure checklists with medical kit locations, EVA readiness gates, and crew exercise scheduling (CFMS). Cross-domain R.I.D.G.E. correlation links cabin and physiological anomalies, missing sensors trigger explicit fault alerts instead of normal values, and alerts clear only after a verified 30-second recovery hold.

On deep-space missions, communication delays and blackouts prevent real-time assistance from Earth flight surgeons during acute events such as hypoxia, CO2 buildup, or solar particle spikes. Running locally keeps triage operational offline and queues telemetry logs for Earth sync when signal returns.
details:
ORION-MED is a crew health and mission support system for long-duration space missions. It combines biomedical telemetry with crew activities and mission events, allowing physiological changes to be interpreted in context rather than as isolated measurements. For example, an increased heart rate during scheduled exercise can be treated differently from the same change occurring during rest.

The system includes crew profiles, biomedical monitoring, alerts, event history, and CFMS, which provides a 72-hour mission timeline and activity schedule. ORION-MED is designed to support both astronauts and mission control, including situations where communication with Earth is delayed or unavailable.

The project focuses on reliability, clear presentation of data, reducing unnecessary alerts, and supporting crew autonomy. Rather than attempting to replace medical professionals, ORION-MED acts as a decision-support system that brings health monitoring and mission planning into one environment.
